text.p: DuPont Co President and Chief Executive Officer John Krol said he expected the company to meet an earnings growth target of 10-12 percent in 1997, and to show record performance this year, with further gains in 1998.

However, Krol told Reuters after the company's annual meeting, potential risk factors include the possibility of new Federal Reserve interest rate increases, coming on top of an already stronger dollar.

Krol told DuPont's shareholders meeting, "Looking ahead, 1997 should be another record year. Assuming the continued health of the U.S. economy and continuing recovery in Europe and Japan, we look forward to an even better 1998."

Krol was asked by Reuters if he thought DuPont would meet in 1997 its long-term financial goals, which include 10-12 percent earnings growth overall and a doubling of revenue growth, to about six to eight percent, in its core chemicals and specialties segment.
"I think the answer is yes, at the moment," Krol said. "We certainly did that in the first quarter, so I'm optimistic."
However, he said, "If in fact they (the Federal Reserve) start jumping the rates...then the U.S. economy is going to turn down on us and we're going to have a struggle."
DuPont, with more than half its sales outside the United States, had taken a "tremendous currency hit" during the first quarter of 1997, Krol said.
Nevertheless, he said, sales in continuing operations in the chemicals and specialties business were up four to five percent in the quarter, on a seven percent growth in volumes.

DuPont aimed to reach the long-term revenue growth target by expanding globally, offering more new products and applications for existing products, expanding alliances, increasing productivity and targeting customers.
Asked at a news conference whether strong first-quarter profit gains at DuPont's Conoco subsidiary had reduced investor pressure to divest the firm, Krol said, "It goes up and down."
"When earnings are good and Conoco is countercyclical...the pressure comes off. When the earnings start to go down, I'm sure we're going to start to hear more pressure again," he said.

Describing DuPont's position regarding its ownership of the unit, Krol said, "I look at Conoco...just like another business in DuPont. And that is that we are looking to have businesses that grow, that exceed the cost of capital.
"So our whole focus has been let's get Conoco to that point. We've done it in the upstream area and we're making progress now in the downstream area."
Asked whether he could rule out a sale, he said, "The facts are, it's just like any other business unit in DuPont. It's got to carry its load. It's got to contribute to our direction."
